question: How should the commons choose its words?
found: Domain-driven design keeps one ubiquitous language used the same way in talk, code and documents - a word with two meanings is a bug. Orwell and the plain-language guidelines ask for the short everyday word a reader already knows, one term for one thing, and no jargon where an everyday word will do. So: look at what others call the thing and what the reader knows, prefer the plain word, keep one meaning, and record the words rejected.

question: How should code be changed so an edit cannot silently miss?
found: Text patches break on formatting: nineteen times a pattern written for one layout met another. Structural tools (ast-grep on tree-sitter, Comby, rust-analyzer's replace) match code as code. Tried on a real bug: ast-grep matched a whole function by its signature and replaced it; it did not see an expression inside a write! macro, because macro insides are tokens. So: replace whole items, keep logic outside macros, put new views in new files, and let every edit stop the job when it does not take.

question: How do people measure repetitive manual work and how draining it is, and decide when to automate it?
found: Site reliability engineering names it toil - manual, repetitive, automatable, without enduring value - and keeps it within a budget. Perceived exertion is rated on one 0-10 scale (Borg CR10); workload can be split into six parts (NASA-TLX), too heavy for every record. Whether automation pays is time per occurrence times frequency (xkcd 1205). Toyota's jidoka makes the machine judge and stop itself, so no person stands by to judge.

question: Read as a database, how sound is ocoeco's data?
found: Measured 2026-11-12 across 22 projects: 14 tables; about 860 links between rows written as text (research 143, sources 317, decided 75, advances 88, touches 104, serves 129, answers 1), of which 2 point at an id found nowhere. Sound in practice, but held together by discipline: no relation is declared, so nothing checks one. Read with tad sql, each project's data already answers joins; what is missing is the shared language saying which field refers to which table, and a check across projects.

question: Does open source have the intelligence and analysis a business has?
found: From the outside, yes: CHAOSS (the Linux Foundation, since 2017) defines metrics of activity and health, and GrimoireLab and Augur gather them from commits, issues, reviews and mailing lists. From the inside, no: why things are as they are, what was decided and rejected, what is needed next, who is doing it, and a way for the people who use the software to see that and take part. That inside is the analysis half of business intelligence and analysis; it is what ocoeco records as the work's own data, oco-agent coordinates, and the observatory presents.

question: What should the board be, taking the best the world has?
found: Kanban (Anderson, from Toyota's production system): make the flow visible, limit work in progress, pull, make policies explicit, measure time. Reinertsen: queues and ageing are the hidden cost. GitHub Projects and Linear: an item is kept once, with fields, and seen through many views - a board is a view, never a second list. Shape Up's hill charts: show uncertainty, not only state. For OCO: the board is a view over every project's backlog - one truth, the data the work already keeps - with the flow open, next, in-progress, waiting, parked, done, dropped; each item in progress held by a driver, with its next step and the day it entered its state; and what needs attention said plainly: a driver holding too much, work with no next step, work that has not moved for a week. oco-agent speaks it; anyone - a person or a machine - pulls from next. Not yet: uncertainty (hill charts), and what someone outside could pick up.

question: How should the data about work be produced so it cannot go stale, and can ocoeco take over what release-please and release-plz do?
found: Measured 2026-11-11: only 224 of 464 recent landed commits across 22 projects (48%) changed any ocoeco data - half of all work leaves no trace in the system. 7 projects use release-please or release-plz; what anything consumes from them is the version and the tag (the conveyor builds binaries from tags, update-pins reads them, crates.io publishing hangs off them); their changelogs (23 to 470 lines of commit titles) drive nothing. Prior art: changesets and Knope record a change's intent when it is made and consume it at release (highest bump wins), but their record is only a bump and a summary, tied to nothing else. Git documents that local hooks can be bypassed (--no-verify); the guarantee has to be at the boundary that cannot be skipped - CI on the pull request, and land.
sources: changesets, knope, githooks, git-trailers, release-please, release-plz

question: What should one recorded look at work be called, in the observatory's language?
found: Observatories keep an observing log; each look is an observation, recorded with its time, target, observer and notes, written at the eyepiece while fresh, and entries point to what they relate to. Weighed: snapshot (already a filesystem and VM word in the author's world - two meanings), exposure (also risk), frame (overloaded in software), observation (exact but long, and it blurs with what the observatory itself does), sighting (seeing someone else's object), entry (says nothing). glimpse: plain, short, one meaning here, and honest that each look is partial - together they make the picture.

question: What should a look back over a stretch of work be called, and what should it hold?
found: The author's word, 2026-11-12, is reflection. Schon showed practitioners learn by reflecting on action; the US Army's After Action Review asks what was planned, what happened, why, and what next; Agile retrospectives are a team ceremony at an iteration's end; blameless postmortems are written after failures. ocoeco needs the plain, general one: anyone - a person or a machine - looking back over any stretch, at any time, about success or failure, saying what they saw, what they learned and what changes.
